oil.summary: Crude softened modestly on the day — WTI -0.24% to $84.26, Brent -0.64% to $90.16 — but the real story is in products: RBOB collapsed 7.59% and Heating Oil shed 5.06%, suggesting demand-side anxiety is overriding geopolitical risk premiums. The bid for crude remains structurally supported by Iran's declared oil blockade and two tankers aborting a Hormuz transit after an incident on the southern lane near Oman, yet prices slipped as other tankers continued passing Bab el-Mandeb. Goldman Sachs flagged diesel as the most acute squeeze, citing the lowest global refining activity since 2020. US senators advanced a bipartisan Russia-Iran sanctions bill including proposed 500% tariffs, adding longer-term supply uncertainty. Japan's Eneos purchasing a rare Canadian crude cargo signals accelerating Middle East diversification by Asian refiners. The month-on-month surge — Brent +23.6%, HO +25.1% — reflects how much geopolitical risk has already been priced in.
drivers: Iran Hormuz blockade: two tankers turned back after incident on southern transit lane, sustaining supply disruption fears
Massive product selloff: RBOB -7.59% and Heating Oil -5.06% on the day, with Goldman flagging diesel crunch at historically low refining activity
US Senate advances bipartisan Russia-Iran sanctions bill with proposed 500% tariffs, raising long-term supply overhang for both producer nations

gas.summary: European TTF surged 4.65% on the day to €60.42/MWh — up an extraordinary 42% over the past month — as the Damietta port drone strike on an Egyptian gas storage tanker and low European storage levels intensified winter supply anxiety. QatarEnergy sent its first LNG cargo through Hormuz in three weeks, a partial relief signal, but Qatar has simultaneously been forced to buy as many as 33 US spot LNG cargoes this year to compensate for disruption at Ras Laffan caused by the Iran conflict. Shell posted $9.8 billion in adjusted Q2 earnings, more than double year-ago levels, directly attributing the result to surging energy prices. US Henry Hub was comparatively muted at +0.59% to $2.741/MMBtu, though down 16.3% on the month, underscoring the wide Atlantic gas price dislocation driven by Middle East conflict.
drivers: Drone strike on gas storage tanker at Egypt's Damietta port and low European storage levels fuel winter supply alarm, lifting TTF +4.65%
Qatar diverting up to 33 US spot LNG cargoes to Asian customers after Iran conflict disrupts Ras Laffan operations, tightening Atlantic LNG availability
Wide Henry Hub/TTF dislocation persists: US gas down 16.3% on the month vs TTF +42%, reflecting geopolitical risk concentrated in European/Asian supply chains

power.summary: EU carbon EUAs were effectively flat on the day at $77.74 (+0.08%), with the market lacking a fresh directional catalyst despite TTF's sharp 4.65% single-day jump. The power complex faces a converging set of structural pressures: scorching heat waves are driving a coal demand and price surge in China, amplifying global thermal fuel competition ahead of a Northern Hemisphere winter. A separate report noted cooling-related emissions are on track to triple by 2050 as heat waves intensify, pointing to a secular increase in power demand. The Trump administration's selection of five Republican-led states for nuclear fuel-cycle hubs could signal incremental longer-term low-carbon generation capacity, though near-term impact is negligible. Overall, the power and carbon data provided today is thin; EUAs are trading in a narrow range while the dominant theme remains gas-price pass-through risk into European power costs.
drivers: TTF +4.65% on the day raises European power generation cost directly, though EUAs showed minimal response at +0.08%
China coal prices and demand surging on heat-wave-driven electricity demand, adding to global thermal fuel tightness
Trump DOE designates five states for nuclear fuel-cycle hubs, a longer-dated signal for domestic low-carbon capacity with no near-term market impact
